name: Nutritional yeast / B-vitamin loading
lead: Nutritional yeast, informally called "nooch", is a deactivated yeast, usually a strain of Saccharomyces cerevisiae, sold as yellow flakes or powder and used in vegan cooking as a cheese-like seasoning [1]. In looksmaxxing and wider wellness circles, "B-vitamin loading" refers to eating nutritional yeast or taking B-complex supplements in generous amounts in the hope of improving skin, hair and nails.

Fortified nutritional yeast can supply several B vitamins in amounts far above the Daily Value per serving, according to manufacturer figures reported on Wikipedia, including thiamine, riboflavin, niacin, vitamin B6 and vitamin B12 [1]. Yeast cannot make B12 itself, so the B12 in such products is added during fortification [1].

No published clinical trial has tested nutritional yeast or broad B-vitamin loading for cosmetic appearance outcomes. Related evidence concerns single nutrients: for biotin, human evidence for hair and nail benefit in people without deficiency is limited, and high-dose biotin can interfere with some laboratory tests [2].
infobox: Fortified nutritional yeast flakes, B-complex supplements

paras: Nutritional yeast is grown for several days on a sugar medium, usually cane or beet molasses, then heat-killed, washed, dried and packaged [1]. It has a nutty, cheesy flavour and is sprinkled on popcorn, potatoes and tofu [1]. It differs from yeast extract and from baker's yeast, which is used for leavening [1].

Manufacturer figures cited on Wikipedia for a fortified product list a 15 g serving as supplying several hundred percent of the Daily Value for thiamine, riboflavin, B6 and B12, and nearly 300 percent for niacin [1]. Unfortified products contain lower mineral and vitamin levels [1].

The practice is discussed as part of nutrition-focused approaches to skin and hair, on the reasoning that B vitamins participate in skin and hair biology and that deficiency can produce visible signs. Biotin deficiency, for example, can cause hair thinning, brittle nails and a facial rash, though dietary deficiency is described as rare [2].

A review cited on Wikipedia found no randomised controlled trials of biotin for hair in healthy people, with improvement reported mainly in case reports of children with genetic biotin deficiency [2]. Evidence for brittle nails comes from small older studies without placebo groups, and a 2018 review described promising results for some nail conditions [2].

High-dose biotin supplements can distort biotin-streptavidin immunoassays, which measure hormones such as thyroid hormones, producing falsely normal or abnormal results; the US FDA issued a safety communication on this in November 2017 [2]. No upper intake limit has been set for biotin by the US National Academy of Medicine or the European Food Safety Authority, because adverse effects of high intake have not been established [2]. Niacin at high intake can cause flushing, a point separate from the cited pages.

card.summary: Eating fortified yeast flakes or stacking B-complex for skin and hair; the vitamins are real, the cosmetic payoff is unstudied.
card.note: High-dose biotin can distort some lab test results.

quick.overview:
Nutritional yeast is a deactivated yeast eaten as a cheesy seasoning, and fortified versions contain large amounts of B vitamins. Some people in appearance communities use it or B-complex supplements hoping for better skin, hair and nails.

No clinical trial has tested the practice for cosmetic results. Evidence on individual vitamins such as biotin is limited in people who are not deficient.
quick.mechanism: B vitamins take part in normal skin and hair metabolism, and deficiency of some, such as biotin, can cause hair thinning, brittle nails or rash. Proponents extend this to the idea that extra intake improves appearance in people who are not deficient; that extension has not been tested in trials.
quick.risks: Nutritional yeast is a food and generally regarded as low risk. High-dose biotin supplements can interfere with some blood tests, including thyroid tests, per an FDA safety communication, and high niacin intake can cause flushing.
